title: Euclid’s view of Messier 78
caption: The star-forming region Messier 78, imaged by ESA’s Euclid space telescope
celestial: Messier 78 · constellation Orion · about 1,300 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre (CEA Paris-Saclay), G. Anselmi

recognition.text: Part of Euclid’s Early Release Observations, May 2024 (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A bright stellar nursery glows at the center of this Euclid view, wrapped in dust and laced with filaments of gas. This is Messier 78, a young star-forming region about 1,300 light-years away in Orion. Near the top shines the bright nebula NGC 2071.

Dark clouds normally hide much of what forms here. Looking in infrared, Euclid saw through them and, for the first time, picked out the smallest sub-stellar objects in Messier 78, some just a few times the mass of Jupiter. Its two cameras found more than 300,000 new objects in this one field.

Counting stars and these lightweight objects, and comparing the two, helps explain how populations of stars form and change. Near the bottom, one filament nicknamed the “traffic light” is a dark nebula forming lower-mass stars along its length. The whole view took about an hour to collect.
scale: Using the source’s listed field of view (41 × 41 arcminutes) and the source’s distance of about 1,300 light-years, the frame spans roughly 16 × 16 light-years. Its light set out about 1,300 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Euclid combined its visible-light camera (VIS) with near-infrared measurements in the Y and H bands from its NISP instrument. Blue shows light at about 0.7 microns, green about 1.1 microns and red about 1.7 microns.
understand.eye: Two of the three colors are near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the mapping was chosen for looks: hot stars read white-blue and dusty regions red.

explore: Brown dwarfs and free-floating “rogue” planets have been suggested as part of the Milky Way’s dark matter. Current knowledge suggests there are too few of them, but the question is open, and Euclid aims to settle it by surveying a large part of the galaxy. The six spikes on bright stars come from diffraction in Euclid’s optics, and a few faint, fuzzy blue circles are “optical ghosts,” ordinary artifacts of a complex optical system that don’t affect the science.
alt: A glowing star-forming region at center, surrounded by dark dust and wispy filaments, with a second bright nebula near the top.
